title: Education
author: How to Teach With AI
summary: The sixth installment of a seven-part series on AI-powered student boards describes a pedagogical practice in which student teams build AI advisory boards representing different disciplinary perspectives, then introduce those boards to each other across subjects and classrooms. The author describes a cross-disciplinary exercise in which an English class's AI board encounters questions from a science class's board, generating metacognitive conversations about how different disciplines frame and evaluate the same real-world problems. The series is grounded in the premise that AI can serve as a scaffold for teaching students to think in disciplinary modes, understanding that physics, history, and literature do not merely study different subjects but approach knowledge and evidence differently. This installment focuses on transfer: how the interdisciplinary AI board encounter helps students recognize their own subject's epistemological assumptions by contrasting them with another discipline's. The design assumes no prior AI expertise from students, treating the board-building process itself as the pedagogical vehicle for developing disciplinary fluency.
points: The student AI board model asks students to curate AI agents representing specific disciplinary perspectives, requiring them to understand what each discipline values, assumes, and how it evaluates evidence.
Cross-disciplinary board encounters produce metacognitive conversations that teacher-led discussion rarely generates: students must articulate why their field frames questions the way it does.

Transfer of learning is notoriously difficult to produce in school settings; the board model generates it explicitly by requiring students to apply concepts from their subject to a framework from another discipline.
When students must explain their discipline's assumptions to another discipline's AI board, they develop a more precise and portable understanding of their own subject's epistemological commitments.

The series treats AI not as a content generator but as a disciplinary lens, and students learn to configure an agent to think like a historian, biologist, or rhetorician, which requires understanding what makes each discipline's reasoning distinctive.
quotes: A student sits down to write a paper for their political science class. Ten minutes in, they realize the paper can't actually be written inside political science. It needs something about the economics of platform markets.

Introducing the Meta-Board The Meta-Board is a new, permanent Board that sits above every class Board your student has built. Its role is to run the conversation between the specialists. Each one has a specific job that no class Board can do.

The computer scientist talks like a computer scientist. The student reads five to seven minutes of pure-voice responses from each Board. Not "they emphasize different things." Where do they actually contradict each other?

The econ Board and the philosophy Board are both using the word 'rational,' but they are referring to different concepts. Here is how the arguments should be rewritten if both Boards want to actually respond to each other." Students who learn to run the Translator become better at any cross-disciplinary conversation they're in for the rest of their lives. The skill of translating between disciplinary vocabularies is the skill of thinking like a generalist.

It's also the assignment most students underperform on, because they've never been taught how. Here's how to run a thesis project with the Meta-Board. At topic selection, the student brings the Synthesis Journal.

The Translator: an advisor who specializes in catching moments when two disciplines use the same word to mean different things, or different words to mean the same thing, and rewriting each claim in terms the other discipline can actually respond to." Page 1
